metrics.label: Precision at a two-week lead time
Usage, billing and support history modelled

problem.label: The problem
problem.lead: The business was losing roughly 6% of subscribers a month,
problem.muted: and nobody knew who until they were already gone.
paragraphs: The retention team had no way to see risk in advance. Outreach was reactive — usually a discount email sent after someone had already asked to cancel, at the point where the decision was made and the conversation was about saving face rather than changing course.
The goal was narrow and testable: predict churn risk early enough that a retention offer could still plausibly work. Anything arriving after the cancellation request was, for this purpose, worthless.

approach.label: The approach
steps: Pulled and cleaned 18 months of customer usage, billing and support-ticket data.
Engineered behavioural features — login drop-off, ticket sentiment, plan downgrades, payment failures.
Tested Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost; picked XGBoost on the precision–recall tradeoff.
Handled class imbalance with SMOTE and threshold tuning rather than the default 0.5 cutoff.
Validated on time-based splits, so no future data was ever used to predict the past.

feature.label: Feature importance
feature.figure: horizontal bar chart — top 8 churn drivers
feature.note: Login drop-off and payment failures dominate; demographic attributes contribute almost nothing, which is why they were dropped from the final model.

tradeoff.label: Key tradeoff
tradeoff.muted: because the two kinds of mistake cost very different amounts.
paragraphs: A false positive costs a discount email to someone who was never going to leave. A false negative costs an entire subscriber. That asymmetry sounds like an argument for recall — but the team had a fixed weekly capacity, and a list padded with low-risk accounts would push genuine risk off the bottom of it.
So the threshold was tuned for a list the team could actually work through, where most names deserved to be there. Recall was allowed to fall.

performance.label: Model performance
performance.note: Performance at the chosen threshold, with the default 0.5 cutoff shown for comparison.

rows.label: Precision on flagged accounts, at a two-week lead time before the cancellation window.
Churn in the piloted segment over the trial period, where the team ran targeted outreach against the flagged list.
A Tableau dashboard the team pulls the risk list from themselves, without asking anyone to write a query.

differently.label: What I'd do differently
differently.mutedA: The weekly batch pipeline sets the floor on lead time.
differently.strong: With more time I'd move the behavioural signals to real time
differently.mutedB: — the model can see a login drop-off days before the batch job does, and those days are the whole product.

handoff.label: Handoff
handoff.note: Risk score, the two features driving it, and the account owner — nothing else.

about.label: About
paragraphs: Prathamesh Kadam is a data scientist based in Galway, Ireland. His work sits between modelling and decision design: building forecasts, churn systems and classification workflows that give teams a clear next action.

Across subscription, retail, support and pricing data, the pattern is consistent: start with the business tradeoff, build the simplest model that can survive production, then hand it over in a way the operating team can actually use.

principles.title: Models with a decision attached
principles.body: Every score needs an owner, a threshold and a clear action. Otherwise it is just another number on a dashboard.

principles.title: Tradeoffs before tuning
principles.body: Precision, recall, cost and capacity get written down before the modelling work starts, so the final threshold is defensible.

principles.title: Handoff is the deliverable
principles.body: The model is only finished when the team can read it, trust it and use it without asking for a query.
